eli5.summary: The group running the network's library was moving its service to a new computer. This note tells users to expect that.

questions: move of the network information center
where did the arpanet information center move
subtitle: Relocation of the Network Information Center services to TYMSHARE

tldr.problem: The Network Information Center (NIC) and its NLS (oN-Line System) services, which held network documentation and information, needed to be transferred from the existing ARC/NIC hardware to a new, more capable system.
tldr.mechanism: ARPANET operators planned to move the NIC's services from the ARC/NIC system at SRI to a new system called OFFICE-1 located at TYMSHARE in Cupertino, California, which would eventually serve ROME, ARPA, and NIC users.
tldr.outcome: User directories were to be transferred to OFFICE-1 once hardware reliability was confirmed, allowing the NIC to continue serving network information needs from a new location.

today: RFC 609 documents a routine but important operational transition in the early ARPANET's infrastructure. The NIC eventually became the foundation for what is now IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) and related RFCs (RFC 620 and RFC 621) address related information center operations.

sections.title: The Move
sections.content:
The Network Information Center (NIC) was the central repository for ARPANET documentation, standards, and network administration information. Its NLS (oN-Line System) provided users with an online interface to query and retrieve network information.

In early 1974, the NIC and NLS operations were being transferred from the existing ARC/NIC system (at SRI-ARC) to a new system called OFFICE-1, which would be installed at TYMSHARE in Cupertino, California. This was a significant operational shift affecting every user of the network's central information service.
sections.eli5: The group that keeps the network's instruction manual was moving to a new computer at a different location.

sections.title: Timeline and Hardware Challenges
sections.content:
The RFC indicates the move would happen "within the next few weeks" of the January 1974 publication date. However, the authors note that TYMSHARE was experiencing hardware difficulties with the OFFICE-1 system at that time. Rather than rush the transfer, the plan was to stabilize the hardware first, then move user directories when reliability was confirmed.

In the ARPANET, network nodes were identified by different numbers in different contexts: OFFICE-1 was site 53 in octal notation (for TELNET) or site 43 in decimal notation (for TIP connections). This notation difference was a common source of confusion in early network administration.
sections.eli5: The new computer was having some problems at first. Rather than move right away, they decided to fix the problems first, then move people's files when it was working well.

sections.title: Communicating with Users
sections.content:
The RFC is itself a notification to ARPANET users that major system changes were coming. Users—including those relying on NIC information services, ROME users, and ARPA users—were advised to watch for future announcements specifying the exact date when their directories and data would be transferred to the OFFICE-1 system at TYMSHARE.

This kind of advance notice was essential in an era before widespread automated system migrations. Network operators needed time to prepare, and users needed warning that their access patterns and connection endpoints might change.
sections.eli5: They told everyone in advance so people wouldn't be surprised when the service moved to a new place.
